catalog_quote: Counting from the end of the word, primary stress predictably falls on the syllable containing the next-to-last vowel. Examples: culi [ˈʧuli] ‘ear’; paa [ˈpaː] ‘thigh’; kaɗaɗi [kaˈɗaɗi] ‘animal’; gorau [goˈrau] ‘young child, toddler’. In careful speech primary stress is clearly heard on the second of two geminate vowels. Compare the following examples. kaancu [kaˈanʧu] ‘there’; paraaso [ˌparaˈaso] ‘to sell’. ... new_statements.quote: Namun, realisasi vokal panjang pada bahasa Lasalimu bukan merupakan fonemis melainkan fonetis semata. Dalam berkomunikasi panjang pendeknya vokal yang diproduksi oleh penutur tidak menjadi hambatan dalam pemahaman satu sama lain. Tampaknya vokal panjang itu terjadi karena pengucapan logat setempat (kolektif idiolek) yang diakibatkan karena terdapat tekanan pada suku kata penultima yang cenderung pengucapan vokalnya agak dipertahankan temponya sehingga terkesan ada perpanjangan vokal tertentu.
new_statements.translation: However, the realization of long vowels in Lasalimu is not phonemic but purely phonetic. In communication, the length or shortness of the vowels speakers produce is no obstacle to mutual understanding. It appears that the long vowel arises from the local manner of pronunciation (collective idiolect), caused by the fact that there is stress on the penultimate syllable, whose vowel tends to be pronounced with its tempo somewhat sustained, so that there is an impression of lengthening of certain vowels.
new_statements.citation: Sanjoko, Yohanis. 2015 [online 2017]. Perbandingan karakteristik fonem bahasa Indonesia dengan bahasa Lasalimu. Kandai 11(1): 55-67. Kendari: Kantor Bahasa Sulawesi Tenggara.
new_statements.locator: p. 64 (PDF page 10 of 13), section 'Kontras Vokal dan Variannya', right column
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (13 pp., text layer; Kandai 11(1), Mei 2015, pp. 55-67, header on p. 1). extracted text of PDF page 10 (printed p. 64) contains the quoted passage word for word: "Namun, realisasi vokal panjang pada bahasa Lasalimu bukan merupakan fonemis melainkan fonetis semata. Dalam berkomunikasi panjang pendeknya vokal yang diproduksi oleh penutur tidak menjadi hambatan dalam pemahaman satu sama lain. Tampaknya vokal panjang itu terjadi karena pengucapan logat setempat (kolektif idiolek) yang diakibatkan karena terdapat tekanan pada suku kata penultima yang cenderung pengucapan vokalnya agak dipertahankan temponya sehingga terkesan ada perpanjangan vokal tertentu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; the stressed penultimate vowel is often held longer, which the author treats as phonetic (non-phonemic) vowel lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The same passage also lists phonetic long vowels in word-final position ([rampu:] 'bakar', [mobu:] 'berat', [ina:] 'ibu') and in the monosyllable [i:] 'di', which the penultimate-stress explanation does not cover; the author does not comment on this.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, in elicited citation forms from a wordlist-based phoneme study (Kecamatan Lasalimu, Kabupaten Buton). The stress remark is made in passing to explain vowel length; the article has no dedicated suprasegmental/stress section and gives no stress-marked examples.
new_statements.identity_note: Sanjoko 2015 describes 'bahasa Lasalimu' as spoken in Kecamatan Lasalimu, Kabupaten Buton, Sulawesi Tenggara = Lasalimu [llm] lasa1237 (Nusi 2012 places the Lasalimu villages in Kecamatan Lasalimu Selatan and Kamaru in Kecamatan Lasalimu). Firman A.D. 2017 treats Lasalimu and Kamaru (Kamaru [kgx] kama1364) as dialects of a single 'Lasalimu-Kamaru' language, as Pusat Bahasa 2008 does, whereas SIL 2006 and Glottolog keep them as two languages; the stress remark quoted is for the Lasalimu variety proper.

new_statements.quote: Counting from the end of the word, primary stress predictably falls on the syllable containing the next-to-last vowel. Examples: culi [ˈʧuli] ‘ear’ / paa [ˈpaː] ‘thigh’ / kaɗaɗi [kaˈɗaɗi] ‘animal’ / gorau [goˈrau] ‘young child, toddler’. In careful speech primary stress is clearly heard on the second of two geminate vowels. [...] kaancu [kaˈanʧu] ‘there’ / paraaso [ˌparaˈaso] ‘to sell’. [...] When a word consists of four syllables, usually secondary stress can be heard on the initial (viz. fourth-from-the-last) syllable. [...] Suffixation precipitates movement of primary stress, but not secondary stress.
new_statements.citation: Mead, David. 2018. Lasalimu word list and notes. Sulang Language Data and Working Papers: Word lists, no. 6 (v2, 28 Nov 2018). Sulawesi Language Alliance, sulang.org. 42 pp.
new_statements.locator: Section 3.2 'Vowels and stress', printed pp. 4-5 (running-header page numbers) = PDF pp. 6-7; exceptions also annotated at word-list items 108 and 110, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 10)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 5140; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Lasalimu word list and notes', author David Mead, 42 pp., text layer). Section 3.2 'Vowels and stress' is on printed pp. 4-5 (running-header numbers) = PDF pp. 6-7, exactly as the reader states. The quoted sentences are all present verbatim (extracted text): 'Counting from the end of the word, primary stress predictably falls on the syllable containing the next-to-last vowel.' with examples culi [ˈʧuli] 'ear', paa [ˈpaː] 'thigh', kaɗaɗi [kaˈɗaɗi] 'animal', gorau [goˈrau] 'young child, toddler'; 'In careful speech primary stress is clearly heard on the second of two geminate vowels.' with kaancu [kaˈanʧu] 'there', paraaso [ˌparaˈaso] 'to sell'; 'When…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (stress on syllable 2 of 2, 2 of 3, 3 of 4 = penultimate) and as Sanjoko 2015's passing remark; adds that the count is by vowel (geminate vowels count as two), the secondary-stress pattern (fourth-from-last / reduplicant-initial), the suffixation shift, and three lexical exceptions (one initial, two vocative-final). Explicitly 'predictable', so non-contrastive.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the syllable containing the penultimate vowel, counting every vowel (each half of a long/geminate vowel counts separately, so in careful speech kaancu is [kaˈanʧu], paraaso [ˌparaˈaso]; in fast speech the whole long vowel may be stressed, [ˈsuːʔe]). Stress is predictable and shifts rightward under suffixation to stay penultimate (kaʔoŋkowulu [kaˌʔoŋkoˈβulu] vs kaʔoŋkowuluno [kaˌʔoŋkoβuˈluno]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: On four- and five-syllable words secondary stress falls on the fourth-from-last syllable (kaʔoŋkowulu [kaˌʔoŋkoˈβulu]); with two-syllable reduplication it falls instead on the first syllable of the reduplicated portion whether that is fourth or fifth from the end (pepunda-punda [peˌpundaˈpunda], limba-limbaʔa [ˌlimbaliˈmbaʔa]); suffixation moves primary but not secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Exceptions beyond the patterns given above are rare in the present corpus.' Named: ɗaoa 'market' with initial stress and shortened medial o, [ˈɗaŏa]; vocative ama 'father' and ina 'mother' with stress and lengthening on the final vowel, [ʔaˈmaː], [ʔiˈnaː] (also annotated at word-list items 108, 110).
new_statements.identity_note: Mead 2018 describes the Lasalimu of the single village officially named Lasalimu, unofficially Lasalimu Pantai (5°15'5.2"S, 123°9'33.9"E), kecamatan Lasalimu Selatan, kabupaten Buton, Southeast Sulawesi, from three speakers (Jabaluddin, Hidayat, Alimuddin) elicited over two days in August 2015 with an 814-item Sulawesi Long List. No other dialect is distinguished.
